utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, The Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we have the appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. It's Carmela Javier, Lorna Bolton, and Mark Harmon for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Daniela Tasic, Chad Mair, Kay Marshall, Colleen Rohan, Milos Androvic, Novak Lukic, and I'm Gregor Guy-Smith on behalf of Mr. Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good afternoon to you out in New York, or good morning, rather, Mr. Sacirbey and everybody down there. Mr. Sacirbey, just to remind you once again that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and fully understood. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. May the record show that we're sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis this afternoon in the absence of Judge Picard who is involved in a another case this afternoon. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sacirbey.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to start my examination for a moment to just deal with what I will call a couple of rules of the road that I hope that we can comply with as we proceed through your testimony for the ensuing period of time. Initially, when I ask you question, I'd appreciate it, to the extent you can, to give me a yes or no answer to the question that I have asked. Obviously if you need to explain that answer, I certainly would have no objection; I would expect you to do so. With regard to another particular issue, because we both speak English, and there's a tendency when two native speakers are speaking in the same language for us speed up in our conversation. I'm going to try, and I know it's a long shot, that we won't do that, but I'm going to wager with you here. And try to -- if we could make a bet with each other to see if we could succeed in not being interrupted by the interpreter in attempt to get us to slow it down, I think that that might be of some assistance, okay?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You've led, sir, from what I can tell, somewhat of a unique and interesting life, and I'd like to spend some time with you talking about how you got to your position as the ambassador. And I understand that you came to the United States as a teenager; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was ten years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And thereafter, you matriculated as we all do, and ultimately ended up in university, I believe, in Louisiana; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what university was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tulane University.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And could you tell us when you went to Tulane University. What was the period of time that you were at Tulane?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there both undergraduate and law school. So I was there from 1974 to 1980.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And after law school, did you remain in Louisiana, or did then journey forth to New York?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came to New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you came to New York, as I understood your testimony, you began working as an attorney for a number of years, and if I'm not mistaken -- well, let's deal with that first. You worked as an attorney for a number of years; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, that is not correct. I came primarily to New York to go to Columbia business school where I had been accepted a year earlier, and in the meantime, I started doing some part-time jobs while I took my bar exam. Upon passing my bar exam, I was offered a full-time position for counsel Standard & Poor's at that time, and continued to complete my M.B.A. at Columbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the work that you were doing as counsel for Standard & Poor's, I understand that you were an investment banker; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at Standard & Poor's, you would not be an investment banker; you would be an analyst reviewing various types of instruments that Standard & Poor's would either issue ratings on or otherwise. I became an investment banker once I left that Standard & Poor's.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During the period that you were at Standard & Poor's, when you were in engaging in financial analysis, I take it that -- were you doing that for any specific sector of the -- of the industry? Or were you just doing general analysis --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially -- I --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, initially, as I said, I was working as counsel for them, so I would a have been really counsel mainly for the debt-rating division, mainly reviewing structure-type financing, but it really -- whatever the requirement was, I was more or less stationed in their offices, even though I was employed by their outside counsel. In fact, Standard & Poor's at that time did not have -- did not have in-house counsel, so in many ways I was de facto in-house counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, when you say you were doing work in debt rating -- in the debt-rating division, is that the kind of work that deals with such things as government bonds?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not -- not -- it may deal with sovereign ratings, yes, but it could have been anything from structured financing to corporate and municipal securities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to the work that you were doing as an analyst, I take it, that's a kind of work that requires some rather meticulous record-keeping, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, most of the time I was not the primary analyst. As I said, I was in fact the attorney reviewing those deals, or in fact I was the head of a department who was overseeing those types of transactions once I relinquished my primary responsibility as counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to your reviewing those deals, I take it that it would be fair to say that you relied on the analyst's work that in fact contained meticulous record-keeping; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- most of the data came from actually the issuer of the debt or the investment banker.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to the -- the question of having the ability to have facts in front of you in order to make determinations of a legal nature with regard to those facts, you relied upon, what I would say is a fair amount of documentary evidence; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Documentary and analytical evidence; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say analytical evidence, you are referring to evidence that also, similarly, is written down; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All right. Now, there's nothing particularly unusual with regard to keeping records in that regard, is there? It's part of the nature and course of the business. True?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I understand your question, and the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And, as a matter of fact, that's something you clearly, if you hadn't learned it in undergraduate school, it is something that you clearly learned while you were in law school, which was the importance of memorializing facts and events. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's something that you then learned in even a more a sophisticated way when you were obtaining your M.B.A., right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And it's something that, certainly, for some period of your life is and -- an exercise that you both personally, as well as professionally, engaged in, and by that I mean, the keeping of records so that you would have a historical account of what occurred; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say "most likely," is there any doubt in your mind that that is something you did during the time that you were both counsel for Standard & Poor's and at a later point in time when you were an investment banker?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you were speaking about both professionally and personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's true, I did ask you the question that way. So let's deal with it, first of all, professionally. With regard to --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, professionally, I feel quite comfortable --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Professionally you feel quite comfortable --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Professionally you feel quite comfortable --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And personally, I'm not asking you --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And personally, I'm not asking whether you kept a diary or not. I'm not attempting to inquire into your personal life in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I think, professionally, I have no doubt that in fact the record-keeping that was undertaken was quite consistent with the responsibilities that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say, "quite consistent with the responsibilities that you had," could you define for us what those responsibilities were?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, when we're talking about my job at Standard & Poor's, again I emphasise most of my career there, I was either counsel where I would not certainly be reviewing the numbers, or I was the head of a department, sometimes the department that was involved in even what was then called new product development, that was analysing new types of ratings in theory. So the actual work on deals usually was done by what was called the lead analyst or the analyst that actually had the direct responsibility for the rating. And that analysis would frequently rely upon information submitted by the issuer of the debt, if it was a debt instrument, or the corporation or, of course, the investment banker that was behind such instruments.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to that work, when you were reviewing the work that was done by the analyst, you were assuming, were you not, that the information that you had was complete, accurate, and reliable?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- that was usually the representation made by the issuer and the investment banker; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And part of your job, certainly at that point in time, in your determination whether to rely upon the analysis which was predicated on facts was your assessment of the totality of that information as being complete, accurate, and reliable. True?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Is one of the things that you -- you analysed during that period of time such things as the expenditures that any particular project that was being presented to your analysts were? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I think I do, and the answer, of course, is that you took those issues at face value that were prevented to you, unless there was some reason to really suspect that the information was inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the manner upon which you would make that determination, and by that I mean suspecting that information was inaccurate, was based upon information that had been supplied to you by your own analysts; correct? I mean, that was one -- it could be one of the manners in which you did that, but it certainly was one.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. By and large you wouldn't have that type of challenge because obviously the issuer, i.e., the investment banker would have a much better understanding of what was involved. Generally, obviously you were conscious of who were dealing with, the more experience had you the individuals involved, the firms involved, the companies involved, the more -- reliant you were upon that information, certainly corporate issuers, municipal issuers. Standard & Poor's, the primary rating analyst dealt with them on a consistent basis. It was not a disjointed relationship. It was a consistent relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And when you moved into the world of investment banking, I take it that the same discussion that we've had thus far would similarly apply. And that by I mean that the information that you had in order to make the determinations that you were going to make with regard to investment banking, required to have complete reliable information.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: By and large, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: By and large, it's -- it's been said that an investment banker is but a gambler who gambles with other people's money because they have no risk to themselves. I don't know whether you share that view or not.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I actually don't. Maybe a less flattering view is that you're a mercenary putting together financing for someone else with -- with obviously no ongoing relationship with that company like a CFO. That's the most unflattering view I can come up with of an investment banker. Otherwise, you are really helping put together a transaction that tends to meet the capital market requirements, and at the same time, tends to meet the issuer's, that is, the -- the institutions that's seeking the financing meets their needs as well. So to some extent it's a Rubik's Cube, where every time you move one element of the deal, something else may come lose. There may be some other need to be addressed. I, frankly, think that if you want to talk about gambling, it's -- it's properly more of a traders job to be that than it is an investment banker's. We viewed our task as being one more of trying to meet the requirements of various parties to the transaction. And generally there were more than two. There was more than just the issuer, and more than just the potential investor or investors.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So it would be fair to say you were involved at that time in what we could say multi-financial considerations?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with regard to the period of time in which you were functioning as an investment banker, that was a time, I think, where it would be fair to say, certainly in the mid-1980s to early 1990s, where the market was quite strong.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lived through the downside of the market as well in the very late 1980s/early 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mm-hm. During the period of time that you were living through the high part of the market, did you deviate from your basic behaviours of -- if I'm characterizing this correctly, of noting information, keeping records of that information, and being in a position where you can rely on that information in the future?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by and large we had actually a very significant department, and I was in charge of that department toward the end of my tenure in investment banking. And that involved significant record-keeping, a lot of individuals associated with that part of the process also working with the bank, we had a credit department that was also part of process, so that it was a multi-faceted effort, consistent with what I think you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Since you were the, as you have just told us, the head of the department, I take it - I'm going to jump forward because you said you also experienced the deadline in the -- in the, I believe, it was late 1980s/early 1990s - that during that period of time, while experiencing the decline, you were able to go back and take a look historically at the investments that you had made to make determinations of what was the most viable and reasonable fashion to proceed financially for your clients.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I know where you're going, and I think that's accurate. But once transactions were issued, then in fact what you had is, on the one side, investors. And on the other side, you had issuers. The investment banker by and large did not have an ongoing fiduciary responsibility, let's say, like a trustee.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, when you discuss the issue of fiduciary responsibility, could you explain to the Chamber what you mean by that term?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have a responsibility to the people on whose behalf you're dealing. In the case of my dealings as an investment banker, the responsibility is actually to the issuer, and, at the same time, I may have legal responsibilities consistent with the laws and regulations at that time to the investor. But I was by and large, as an investment banker, employed by the issuer.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say employed in the context of being employed for that particular function. Of course, my -- my employer was the bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to what you've just said in terms of your last answer, you said I may have legal responsibilities consistent with the laws and regulations at that time to the investor. With regard to the general notion of a fiduciary duty that one has, would it be fair to say that is something that you considered to be an aspect of your work independent of your work as an investment banker? And by that I'm obviously referring to the work that you did later in your life when you became the ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. As I understand your particular narrative or your story, there came a point in time in your life when you were asked to be of assistance to the burgeoning state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, financially.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asked to assist in potential economic transformations as well as the political transformation, before the division of the former Yugoslavia. I was never asked to be in any sort of fiduciary or other capacity at that time. It was purely as someone who had insight into the free-market system, particularly the US market system. Perhaps because I had some understanding of what was happening in the US, both in the economic and political context. Certainly the notion of a burgeoning Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent state was not, at that time, I think, really the issue. At that time it was hoped for by, I think, a lot of people in the former Yugoslavia, at least certainly system of them, under the leadership of some of the regional leaders, that the former Yugoslavia might in fact manage to restructure itself and maintain some sort of confederal or other lose federal arrangement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. But, and that's not a critical "but." But part of the reason that you became involved with the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time was due to your expertise in the area of investment banking. True?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you'll probably to have ask those people who sought my engagement, and I must admit that my engagement, probably until the year 1992, was, at best, intermittent.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There came a point in time when your engagement shifted from being intermittent to being more constant; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. When you say that your engagement was intermittent prior to 1992, could you tell us what precise, and I'm assuming that you were engaged in financial advice at that time to the Bosnian government, you gave?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, I think that would be giving myself too much credit. I happen to sit in on the meeting with the World Bank directorate that included the former Yugoslavia in Washington. Maybe I had one, two, three, conversations with President Izetbegovic in a six-month term. Probably starting in February of 1992, when I was asked to arrange a meeting with the Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali at that time and Mr. Cyrus Vance is when my engagement become a little bit more consistent, although I continued to in fact pursue my career as an investment banker along with my partners.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And when you were asked to arrange that initial meeting in February of 1992, was that predicated upon your familiarity with matters financial, or was that predicated on something else, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was predicated on the idea that -- well, yes, I guess that's a fair question. First of all, I'm not sure necessarily why I would have been asked, expect that clearly I lived in New York, I was an attorney, I knew English and knew my way around the financial and business and legal community here probably better than any other Bosnian. But that may not be saying very much. There were not very Bosnians at that time who were living outside the country. That happened only obviously as a consequence of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Above and beyond that, there was another reason, was there not, and that is, if I might use some of your language, very simply put, My father and President Izetbegovic were old friends from the Young Muslim's group?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. And my mother was also, frankly, a part of that group, and she was also friendly with President Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, when you referred to the --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: By then, I should add, by then my mother had passed away. That's why she is not mentioned in the context of this narrative.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, my -- my condolences to you today as much as yesterday, when one's mother passes away, it is something that leaves quite a hole in one's life.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: She certainly left more than just an emotional hole in my life. She was a guiding light. She was a very progressive women, a the same time managed to deal with her theology and her ideology and her profession, I think in an extremely positive manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, we share that experience, Mr. Sacirbey. We share that experience.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to talk to you for a moment about the issue of the Young Muslims group. Now as I understand it --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As I understand it your father spent, and I believe your mother may have as well, spent some time in -- in jail with President Izetbegovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton. Sorry, Mr. Sacirbey. Mr. Sacirbey, sorry, there's -- the Prosecutor is on her feet. Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm just wondering what the relevance of Mr. Sacirbey Senior's and President Izetbegovic's involvement in the Young Muslims organisation has to any of the material issues at trial. It's not a matter that was raised during examination-in-chief, so unless it relates somehow to Mr. Sacirbey's credibility, it has no relevance in my respectful submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There is replete in Mr. Sacirbey's testimony discussions with regard to the issue of perceptions concerning Muslims, and perceptions concerning multi-ethnic society. With regard to this particular information this is but a prefatory question as it relates to not only that particular issue, which is the issue of the creation ultimately of a Muslim state, or not, but also to the issue of the perception outside of what the intent may have been, the outside perception of the world. And, to the extent that Mr. Sacirbey's father was involved as a Young Muslim, it has some bearing with regard to how those issues were perceived years later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the question had to do with having Mr. Sacirbey senior having spent time in jail with President Izetbegovic, so that had nothing to do with perceptions of the outside world. And we heard nothing in Mr. Sacirbey's testimony about perceptions of the outside world in terms of establishing some kind of a Muslim state. This is nothing that arises out of examination-in-chief, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I respectfully disagree. This whole issue -- this whole issue is an issue that threads through this case. And probably the argument would take longer than the answers that the brief questions had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My only concern, Mr. Guy-Smith, is that you're talking about Mr. Sacirbey Senior's membership of the Muslim's youth group, not Mr. Sacirbey here. And I'm not quite sure whether outside perceptions of ethnicity, as you say, in -- in measures of the Bosnian state that, perhaps, may emanate from his father. Are you suggesting that they are transferrable to him, or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, there are a couple of things that I wish to explore, and perhaps the answer will be no. I have no way of knowing what the answer will be. But among other things, I do believe that Mr. Sacirbey's father at one point was part of the mission at the UN. And I do believe his father wrote letters to the UN with regard to the position of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And are those letters --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Whether or not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you attributing those letters to this Mr. Sacirbey?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you attributing Mr. Sacirbey's father's letters to Mr. Sacirbey?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I will find out a later point in time whether or not he is aware of them or not. So far he has adopted every letter that was written on behalf of his delegation. I don't know whether or not he is going to move away from the letter that his father wrote or not. I would assume that he would not. But to the extent that there is a political issue here and to the extent that we have been accused of, among other things, being prejudiced against Muslims, to the -- the issue with regard to a philosophy that may well have been shared, may well not have been shared, but once again, as I said before, the argument takes longer than the questions. He may reject it entirely, at which point, we will all be satisfied. But the extent to which there was a philosophy taught and shared by Mr. Sacirbey who is before us is something that I wish to explore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Mr. Guy-Smith, I think it is a bit far-fetched to be dealing with his father. If you talk about --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well, I'm not going to -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think it is irrelevant. The objection will be upheld.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you were asked to become involved with the government, I take it that it would be would be fair to say that part of the reason that you were asked to become involved was predicated upon the shared history of your father and President Izetbegovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's accurate. Although, again, I think, President Izetbegovic would have better answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, that may well be the case, but I don't believe that he is in a position to do so.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I'm sure --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I think -- I think your assessment is probably fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And in that regard, and now I'm moving forward but a bit, would it be fair to say that one of the principles that was historically espoused by Mr. Izetbegovic dealt with the importance of the Islamic struggle? Again, I think you know what I'm referring to, because obviously the Islamic declaration for which he was jailed.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. I think -- I think, first of all, it would be inaccurate to term it the "Islamic struggle." I think it is more about the Islamic identity, and obviously a Europe that is in many ways very different than other Islamic countries or different from Islamic countries. And in a situation where Bosniaks or Bosnian Muslims obviously had both a very much European identity, if you would. One based upon Euro-Atlantic cultural and political values and, also at the same time had an Islamic identity. I think the notion of some sort of struggle, political struggle, struggle of -- I'm not sure what that term is meant to imply. And I would just ad here that in hindsight it is very easy to see that in my engagement I probably saw the survival of that Islamic identity in Bosnia very much consistent with the American model of a multicultural society. And I think many of us had hoped that the former Yugoslavia would have achieved those types of results as well. In hindsight it probably failed on that point, or at least to some extent it failed. And I think the United States still continues by and large to uphold its multi-ethnic identity. And as do other societies, but, of course, my greatest experience is with the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. What you did share with President Izetbegovic, and this is a question that I'm asking, was your distaste for the communist regime under Tito. Now, you, of course, would have been a child, but that is something, I take it, that was taught to you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it's word distaste requires a certain definition here. Yes, we were refugees; in fact, political refugees from the former Yugoslavia. And as you have noted, my parents both were jailed by that regime. But at the same time we continued to have friends from not only the former Yugoslavia but even friends from that regime who were in positions of authority, including the former Yugoslav ambassador to Washington.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to the question that I had asked you before, I was relying on, I believe, its language from the Islamic declaration, which was a document that was penned by Mr. Izetbegovic, I believe, in the 1970s; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I was relying on the following. And so you know what I was thinking at the time. And perhaps you agree and perhaps you don't, which is --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Does my friend have a copy of the document for us?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It is but one quote. I don't have the document, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm not sure how I can follow along and be satisfied that the text is being quoted accurately if there's not a copy available.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'll get you a copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Which is: "In the struggles for the Islamic order, all means are permissible except one: crime. No one has the right to defile the good name of Islam by the uncontrolled and superfluous use of force. Is that something you're familiar with having been said by President Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say to you I never read the Islamic declaration as a whole. I didn't even -- frankly, wasn't particularly concerned of its existence or wary of its existence until it was raised in -- in political discussions. I am aware of some of these direct cites, and I have even questioned President Izetbegovic on some of these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard -- with regard to your questioning of President Izetbegovic on some of these issues, did you ever discuss with him the following view? That: "The Islamic order can only be established in countries where Muslims represent the majority of the population. If this is not the case, the Islamic order is reduced to mere power as the other element in Islamic society is missing and may turn to violence. The non-Muslim minorities within an Islamic state, on condition that they are loyal, enjoy religious freedom, and all protection."

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever I discussed this matter with President Izetbegovic, and certainly was not more than two, three occasions during obviously a vision of what Bosnia would like, he made it very clear to me, and, of course, we can all then question whether he was sincere or not, I believe he was sincere, that in fact he was looking to have Bosnia take on the character of a secular state, not an Islamic state, not a state dominated by any one ethnic or religious group, not dominated by any theology or ideology beyond that consistent with its European neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you discuss with President Izetbegovic any concerns that might be raised about some of the historical positions that he had taken with regard to Islam in the modern world, even in light of what you just said about your -- your perception of his view?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clearly, if you're raising the issue now, the issue was raised before on numerous occasions what in fact did President Izetbegovic stand for. And from my perspective it was very important that he stood for a multi-ethnic secular society not dominated either, on the one hand, by theology, or, for that matter, on the other hand dominated by some sort of atheist ideology. Clearly to me again, America served as the most appropriate model. And with all due respect to the others who are represented this Court, I believe there other modern societies, although not perfect, who would fit that model as well, of that is a progressive, multi-ethnic secular state.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I understand what you're saying here, and my question and the thrust of my question is slightly different. Recognizing the existence of this discussion, which is the discussion concerning whether or not Bosnia and Herzegovina was going to be a Muslim state or a multi-ethnic state, with regard to the issue of the perception of the outside world. Is that a matter that you discussed, first of all, with President Izetbegovic, as to how you were going to --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And with regard to how that -- the perception of the outside world was going to be dealt with, in terms of this issue, which is, I believe, somewhat of a sensitive issue, and somewhat of an important issue in terms of the, not only the conflict, but the history of the creation of a state, did you formulate a plan as to how to deal with the potential negative perception?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I think the substance is as important as the perception. And I must say that, yes, there were times when I raised issues not only of perception but substance. I was very much influenced by what I call Bosnia and Herzegovinian patriots who were not Muslims and how much they had committed to the struggle from politics to the battlefield. For example, General Jovan Divjak, who was a Serb, was one of the main defenders and was one of the chief military commanders of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I always felt that his contributions were not only significant, but in fact they were indicative of what a new Bosnia and Herzegovina could look like and should look like. It was also, frankly, my view that people like General Jovan Divjak who, as I understand it, have testified before the Tribunal in the past, was someone who had a choice. He could give in to what I would call ethnic impulses, and decide that in fact he was going become part of some sort of nationalist Serbian agenda, or in fact he could continue to support what I believe was the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that is as a progressive pluralistic democratic state. I think if you want to ask me what were President Izetbegovic's shortcomings in this way, it is very simple. He was someone who had lived all of his life in the former Yugoslavia. So unlike myself, or for that matter my family, he never had the opportunity to experience what it meant to live in a progressive, democratic, as well as pluralistic society. Although I think Yugoslavia certainly deserves credit for being a multi-ethic society, clearly was not democratic, and I think we can question to what extent it was progressive.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you for -- for your answer. And I understand that you have mentioned one individual who you found great comfort, and I don't use the word lightly, in terms of being a forward thinker. But my question was, did you devise a programme -- I supposed you dealt with the substance, but you haven't dealt with the issue. Did you devise a programme whereby the perception of an Islamic state being created was to be -- I'm going use the word defeated here or to be explained away, other than just by saying it was being to be multi-ethnic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think again, you're trying to maybe find a distinction between the substance versus the presentation, and I certainly did not see that there should be any distinction before that. To the extent that one had to answer accusations, maybe that would be a response to that, but I believe the substance was as or more important than the presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. We will come -- we will come back to this issue in terms of some of the allies that you found yourself with as the years progressed, okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me understand the question. I know it has been answered, Mr. Guy-Smith, but just for my own understanding. In that previous question, you were asking for plans for an Islamic state being created and in the same breath characterizing that state as multi-ethnic. On the face of it, those two terms sound contradictory. Was that in fact Izetbegovic's characterization? He called it an Islam state?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if you -- and perhaps my question is -- is too wordy. The substance of my question is, did they devise a programme to defeat the perception, to change the perception of the outside world that they were creating an Islamic state?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I want to go back now in -- in time to when you first began your work. Could you tell us when that was? And by your work, I'm talking about your work as an ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officially I was appointed by President Izetbegovic on May 22nd, 1992, which was on the day that Bosnia and Herzegovina was admitted to the United Nations. I probably was more consistently active for a month or two or three before then, depending, of course, on the situation. When Sarajevo became besieged in early April, clearly the work intensified. I worked closely with Dr. Haris Silajdzic who was a foreign minister of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time. And I presented my credentials a couple of weeks, maybe ten days after, actually, Bosnia was admitted to the Secretary-General formally.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you first began working as the representative, the work that you did was out of your law office; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was actually out of my business office which was on 6th avenue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you stayed in your business office for, if I'm not mistaken, a period of approximately four months; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, give or take a couple of months.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during the period of time that you were there at -- at your first office, you had some difficulties, as I understand it, setting up an account because you did not have a tax ID number; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And that would have been an account for the Bosnian government; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been an account for the mission of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Because I was a US citizen and I did not wish to relinquish my US citizenship, I, frankly, saw my work on behalf of Bosnia as being temporary and that I would return to my American life. I in fact was in an unusual capacity of having dual citizenship but within the United States, even though it was before the United Nations representing, obviously, a different country, that is -- the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I was going say that my colleague -- I was going to say that I see that Ms. Bolton has risen, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You rose a bit late. In the middle of the answer, I couldn't stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: No, I understand. And I just wish to indicate that I think if this line of questioning is going to continue at all, we should probably go into closed session because the relevance of it would relate only, I think, to the allegations that are currently out of Bosnia and Herzegovina, unless there is some other relevance my friend is suggesting that I'm not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, there is some other relevance that I think exists with regard to this particular issue. Would you like me I explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know whether your colleague would like you to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Whether or not she would like me to -- well -- fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm prepared to take your word for it. I don't know whether she wants to know the relevance so that she follow you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I have idea what the relevance would be other than what I have already stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I'm unclear as to what Ms. Bolton's concern is, to be perfectly honest with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Well, my concern is that if my friend is saying there is some other relevance to it, then I say it is not relevant. If my friend is saying that it is relevant to the allegations, then I'm asking him to go into closed session. But I can't tell the Court which my position is until I know what my friend is saying in terms of what the relevance is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... you might have explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. My confusion is this somewhat ambiguous term that's being used, which is the allegations. I'm not particularly clear about what Ms. Bolton concern is as of yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe if you just articulate the standpoint from which you regard them as relevant, she will know and then can decide whether or not she wants to go in private session or to stay in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Sure. The issue for the moment is but an issue of record-keeping. That's all it is for the moment. At a certain point in time it may change, at which point, then, I think she probably would be right, and -- well, I'm not sure -- excuse me, you know what? As a matter of fact, I don't believe it is appropriate to go into closed session in any event. Mr. Sacirbey -- excuse me, I apologise, Mr. Sacirbey has an attorney present. And if the attorney is concerned --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- with regard to any issues that make expose Mr. Sacirbey to criminal liability, then the attorney who is present can raise those issues. As I understand Ms. Bolton's position, Madam Bolton is now acting as an attorney for Mr. Sacirbey. And if that is the case, that is inappropriate. This is something that we visited once before. But irrespective of the issue of the relevance of the question, whether or not this is an appropriate utilisation of going into closed session is an entirely different issue. What is the interest here that is being protected by the Prosecution? If what we are looking for, assuming the worst of all possible worlds for Mr. Sacirbey, and I don't believe we're at that stage right now, but assuming that that is the case, then this is the kind of information, this is the kind of truth that should be not only presented to the Chamber but presented to the world, if that's an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm actually referring to the issue that was the subject of the Prosecution's motion with respect to limits on cross-examination. And at paragraph 21 of the Court's ruling, it actually indicates that we had raised a number of concerns about public discussion of these allegations because of the fact that Mr. Sacirbey would have certain rights, right to remain silent, for example, if he were asked some of these questions in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And the protection that the Court noted in its judgment, one of the protections was that Sacirbey and the Prosecution are free to request private or closed sessions when the circumstances so require. So in answer to my friend' suggestion that it is not appropriate for the Prosecution to ask to go into closed session, I'm doing so because Your Honours' ruling specifically indicated that it would be appropriate. And this is, as far as can I tell, again, an issue where the only relevance of his record-keeping is with respect to the allegations that have been made by Bosnia and Herzegovina. And again my concern is, as I articulated in the original motion, that the subject not be discussed in a context where the authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina would have the advantage of obtaining information as a result of these proceedings that they wouldn't have a right to otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might say something briefly, or should I wait for -- I think I should probably wait for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going to have the last world.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm clear about that. I'm absolutely clear about that. I in no way whatsoever wish to -- you would assume for any purposes whatsoever that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, you go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My concern really does remain the same, which is that the Prosecution, at this time, is taking the place instead of the able gentleman who is sitting in the room in New York with Mr. Sacirbey as his attorney. And I'm sure that if he has any concerns, he will raise them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On that one, I would, under normal circumstances, I would agree with you 100 percent. But if we have a decision that authorised both the attorney sitting there and the Prosecution to asked for closed session, then we are bound by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate that, and I know that you're going to have the last word. Reading that decision, it says when the circumstances require. The best individual who make such a determination is Mr. Sacirbey's lawyer because is he there for purposes of protecting the interests of his client against the -- against -- because he has a privilege against self-incrimination. It is not the Prosecution. The Prosecution is running interference in seeking to keep the truth from the public by doing it in this fashion. If Mr. Sacirbey did not have an attorney and the Prosecution chose to stand in such shoes, then I might take a different position and have a different view of it. But concerning that he has an attorney there, I respectfully suggest that when the attorney wishes to make such an objection, the attorney will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you -- that is tantamount to ask for reconsideration of that decision, Mr. Guy-Smith, which we cannot do at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, my objection obviously is noted for the record, then, and I understand the Court's ruling. I think it is an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is appropriate. Just for the sake of the record, then the objection -- let the record show that the objection is upheld on that basis. That would be an appropriate time to take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, what I'd like to do is I'd like to ask my next question. And then before Mr. Sacirbey answers that question, we can make a determination of whether or not we need to go into private or closed session, and then we'll take it from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You had mentioned that the account to be opened was an account for the Bosnian -- for the mission of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and as I understood your answer, but because you were a United States citizen, there were some difficulties in opening such an account. Is that correct, will be my question. And before you answer that question, I will see whether or not either your counsel or the Prosecution believes that question should be a question that should be attended to in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, this line of questioning only has relevance to the allegations arising out of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so, in my respectful submission unless there is some other relevance that my friend wants to explain, I would ask for a closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I tend to disagree with Ms. Bolton. But for purposes of ease, because I'm not going telegraph all of that, which I'm thinking, we can go into closed session -- or private session, I apologise. Private or closed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber move into a -- do you want private or closed session?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The ruling says either, at your discretion, Your Honour. So I'm in your hands. I would ask for closed but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Closed means we drop the drapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The difference between the two has just been explained to me, so private session will do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Private.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUIRGUIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, this is Peter Guirguis. Just so I might understand, what is the difference?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The difference is that closed session, even the identity of the witness -- the witness would not be seen by the public. What -- in private session, everybody can see him, but they don't hear what we say, all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUIRGUIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now I want to turn for a moment to some issues with regard to your contact with the Office of the Prosecutor in two instances initially, and then we will expand from -- from there. Before testifying in the instant case, you met with members of the Prosecution team, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And do you recall when you met with them?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the case which you are standing on, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Sacirbey.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met actually on two separate occasions. And I'm going to only give you general basis as best as I can, and they happen to be -- I think in both -- once in 2008 it was for approximately a week, actually, a work week, and I think that was at the end of April, beginning of May of 2008. And also with respect to this year, it was about the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say -- when you said that you met for a work week, do I take it to mean that you met with the Prosecution for five days? Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the last time it was three or four days, and it was more or less for the workday; that is, let's say, 9.00 to 5.00, generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And the time before that when you met with him in 2008, was that for a full work week?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was also for four days, if I'm not mistaken. We envisaged maybe Friday, but that day, apparently, was a necessary -- again, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And as you sit here today, at the time that you met with them in 2009 and 2008, were those conversations tape-recorded?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they were, at least on one occasion that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And who was present during those tape recordings, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first instance it was Mark Harmon, who should be in the court with you, and hello, Mr. Harmon. And Mr. Brett Randall. In the second instance it was -- again, Mr. Brett Randall, who obviously is not immediately there at the ICTY, and Ms. Lorna Bolton, of course, who is also there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do I understand that when you are talking about the first instance and the second instance, you met with Mr. Harmon and Mr. Randall in 2008. And you met with Ms. Bolton and Mr. Randall --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in which of those sessions were you tape-recorded?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember certainly in 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. And did you have an opportunity to review that tape-recording prior to coming to testify here today?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]

I certainly was comfortable with it being on or off.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand. With regard to meetings that you have had with the Office of the Prosecutor, this is not the first time, however, that you met with the Office of the Prosecutor in relation to a pending case here at the ICTY, is it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not. I've certainly had, if you want to call, phone conversations. I've had those types of discussions, and, of course, I have had person-to-person meetings. And I believe you referred to one of those, which was Sir Geoffrey Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the prosecution of Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And during your conversation with Sir Geoffrey Nice, could you tell us what year that occurred in.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was September 2004, but I also met -- or I shouldn't say met. We had discussions over the phone at least two extensive discussions, two -- either late 2002 and certainly 2003, early 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the face-to-face meeting that had you with Mr. Nice, also present during those meetings was Mr. Randall; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the -- in the face-to-face meeting, yes, Mr. Randall was there. I should also emphasize just to be complete. I have had numerous meetings with the ICTY office, particularly the Prosecutor's office during my diplomatic tenure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. We'll get to that particular subject. utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the other being in the Perisic matter; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the Milosevic -- with regard to the Milosevic matter, those interviews were all tape-recorded; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. That's just a --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That just a --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's been awhile, and I just frankly -- please continue. I'm having --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure, I understand. With regard to those particular matters, but that I'm referring to the tape-recorded meetings you had with Sir Geoffrey Nice, have you had an opportunity to review or listen to those tapes?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I have ever had an opportunity to listen to any tapes. And I do not believe that I reviewed any transcript of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And, I take it, the same is true, and I think you may have already answered this question, but just to wrap up this particular issue, that of taping and transcripts, that, with regard to the meeting that had you with Mr. Harmon in which you were tape-recorded, you have not had an opportunity to either listen to the tape or review that transcript either; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm quite sure I didn't have a chance to listen to any tape. I don't believe I have had a chance to review certainly the transcript in full, if there was one. I have had a chance certainly to review elements of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to, once again, Mr. Randall's involvement in your particular life as it related to the Milosevic case, you exchanged a series of e-mails with Mr. Randall concerning your potential testimony; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to the issue of you being held in custody for a year and a half, could you just give us the dates that you were held in custody without any further discussion about it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a pretty broad question. I think what I would just say is that the word -- that it was clear from our discussions that there would be a rebuttal stage that would be forthcoming, that in fact the direct stage was already either completed or to be soon completed. Again, I'm speaking of September 2004, toward the end. I'm sure you can check from the record that when direct was completed -- and I just can't recall what all the impediments were for my direct testimony and what all the opportunities were for my rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you in your conversation with Mr. Nice have a discussion about specifically what evidence would be sought from you prior to you giving Mr. Nice any information about the facts?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- no, I think -- I think you're suggesting that Mr. Nice approached me with a request of what evidence I should or maybe could provide, and I think it was a rather very broad discussion of issues that I think certainly could be seen in many different lights, in terms of my role as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I -- discussion took place over three very long days.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand that. With regard to your last answer, I'm going to read to you from a transcript that was provided to the Defence and see whether you can confirm or deny the following statement being made by Mr. Nice to you concerning the issue that we are now talking about.

utterances.text: Can my friend assist me with a tab number in the binder as provided.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]

utterances.text: Yes, there is. I just wanted to make sure that the interpreter had a chance to finish interrupting. With regard to the discussion that you had with Mr. Nice, it would be fair to say, would it not, that that is a quite focussed discussion, as opposed to the general discussion that you had suggested moments ago, that Mr. Nice in fact was looking for very specific information to come from you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That very well may be a reading of what have just looked at. But frankly, I'm of the view that that was the very broad discussion relating to many facts. utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, indeed so, and we will be discussing that, sir. utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: But are you suggesting that I'm some sort of initiator of this endeavour? I obviously may be a witness or even an interested party. But I'm not sure I would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
