utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm suggesting that Mr. Nice was the initiator.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that may or may not be. But I think you're asking me characterize his statements here in a way that maybe I didn't quite see it the same way. Although, clearly, I would have been -- I don't think the word is necessarily sympathetic, but I certainly would have been someone who had been paying attention to the types of evidence that could in fact provide the result that's discussed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That I appreciate, but that is it not the thrust of my question at this time. The thrust of my question at this time is really --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- much more discrete. With regard to the other issue, as you've raised, we will have that discussion a bit later. If we could, moving to the next page, there's a continued discussion between -- well, actually, what it is, is a statement by Mr. Nice to you about what the Prosecution is interested in obtaining from your participation in this case. And I'm referring you now to page 4, line 11. "Bearing in mind" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, in this case on the monitor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And starting at line 11, through line 33, there's a discussion, is there not, with regard to a series of conceptual issues, as they related to the facts in the Milosevic case, that Mr. Nice shares with you, for your comment.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way I understand this paragraph reading again, again, I don't remember the firsthand discussion; it's been a while. But that certainly sounds consistent with the interview that we had. As can you see also, from what I can quickly tell, most of the time I'm either answering with either with one sentence or one-word answers. But I believe the reference here is to, obviously, the massacre in Srebrenica, to what extent it links the actual perpetrators --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You're missing my point.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... the perpetrators to Belgrade, and potentially others that were either --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You're missing my point here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You were once again directed by Mr. Nice towards evidence that he was interested in you speaking to. And, as you said, you gave monosyllabic answers, for example, on page 4, at line 1: "Right." Now the "right" there is with regard to an understanding of what Mr. Nice wanted from you. Correct? You're acknowledging -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... excuse me, sir.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You're acknowledging the -- the statement made by Mr. Nice with regard to the information he requires from you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me, did I understand what he was saying to me, the answer is yes, right. If you're asking me, do I agree with any particular agenda, I -- I can't say as to what you believe that agenda may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I guess that's what I'm really having trouble with.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah, you're making an assumption, my friend. Which --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- is unfortunate. If you choose to second-guess the question, then you will find yourself in a bit of a dilemma. I'm asking a very simple question with regard to the information that's contained on the page.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, if you're asking me if Sir Geoffrey had in fact read out certain views or perspectives of the Prosecution and I was informed of those, then the answer is, of course, yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. You also discussed with Mr. Nice various witnesses that the Defence might call; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And, as a matter of fact, there came a time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. I'm trying not to object unnecessarily. But have I been listening to this line of questioning and thinking my friend was going somewhere with it, and I'm just not clear on the relevance of the 2004 interview of Mr. Nice is to the issues before this Tribunal. And maybe I'm just missing something, but perhaps my friend could indicate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The topic matter is discussed by Mr. Nice with Mr. Sacirbey in 2004, in large measure, covered issues that are being addressed in this trial. And I think that, for example, the discussion that we have just gone through with regard to Mr. Nice's intent to obtain particular information with regard to the participation of the VJ is, to put it bluntly, a central issue in this trial, if not the central issue in this trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, maybe I wasn't clear enough. I guess what I'm not understanding is what the relevance is of the parts of the transcript that my friend has put to the witness. You know, I understand what the relevance of any substantive matters he discussed with Mr. Nice, and if there are any inconsistent statements in those matters, those would certainly be relevant. But unless is he alleging some kind of wrongdoing on the part of Mr. Nice, then this line of questioning doesn't seem to have any relevance, as far as I can tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, if I might, so terribly briefly, I think that Ms. Bolton is somewhat rushed in her concern. Whether or not the Defence will be attributing a prosecutorial misconduct at any point in time to the Office of the Prosecutor in general or Mr. Nice in specific is an issue that, if it is to be addressed, will be addressed at a later point in time. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, I thought you were finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At this point in time, all that is being done is the facts are being developed with regard to the interview process that occurred between Mr. Sacirbey and Mr. Nice as it relates to a general intent and plan of information that the Office of the Prosecutor chose to obtain from Mr. Sacirbey. Now, I wish to take it -- and once again, and I do apologise to Mr. Sacirbey, because his concerns are distinct from the concerns that exist for this trial. So if this argument is to proceed any further, I'm going to ask that it be done outside of his presence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: My concern, Your Honour, was that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, once again --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Oh, I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I'm going to ask this matter be continued outside of his presence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, out there in New York, are you able to mute --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I will do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. Tell us when you have done.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] It's muted now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me try an experiment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just find out. Are you reducing the volume, or are you muting? Everything has gone dead now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Like me try an experiment, like they say in the Verizon commercial. Can you hear me now? Apparently no, so I think we've got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You made proceed then. Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I actually asked Mr. Harmon to step out of the courtroom to retrieve some case law that we were actually looking at earlier today which had to do with the extent to which the Defence can get into areas of preparation of witnesses and prosecutorial misconduct without a formal application. And I don't want to misstate the case law because it was something I just reviewed today. And I would ask for indulgence for perhaps two minutes while he comes back with the book that I was looking at earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are we discussing the issue of case law here at the Tribunal or case law generally or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: At the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, we'll wait.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm looking at Mr. Tarculovski's book, "Jurisprudence of the International Criminal Courts and European Court of Human Rights." He has -- he is citing actually a decision of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda for the following proposition: "A presumption exists that counsel perform their duties in accordance with the ethical principles that govern the legal profession" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Speakers are kindly asked to read a little bit slower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are kindly asked to read slowly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: That was -- I'll slow down. JUDE MOLOTO: {Overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... if we might, if we could have the name of the case or the date of the decision, that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I will cite that at end. "This includes counsel's conduct during preparatory meetings with witnesses. Unless a party makes a specific allegation of misconduct on the part of counsel, in which case the allegation must be substantiated, questions that generally tend to probe into the details of communication between a lawyer and a witness during pre-testimony preparations would, if allowed by the Chamber, render the presumption negatory. Accordingly questions relating to pre-testimony meetings between the Prosecutor and witnesses, while permissible, must in the absence of any substantiated allegation of misconduct be limited to the number of such meetings, the dates of the meetings, and their duration." And that is case is Prosecutor versus Bizimungu Augustin et al. It was a decision on a motion pursuant to Rule 73 released -- says, "raised during the 3rd March 2005 hearing." And it looks like the decision date was the 1st of April, 2005. And the case number was ICTR-00-56-T. I think that's the citation for my friend. Again, simply my concern is that we're going into the substance of those preparatory meetings which really are relevant if my friend is making a substantiated allegation and Mr. Nice in focussing Mr. Sacirbey's attention on certain issues, but before he can go there, he has to formally make that allegation and Your Honours have to rule that it is substantiated. Otherwise, according to at least this decision, there's at least persuasive authority for Your Honours to find that it's not a proper area of examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think -- there are a couple of things that I now find quite noteworthy. First of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Noteworthy. First of all, it's as Mr. McFarlane said many years ago, Curious strange that the Prosecution would be engaged in research on the issue of its misconduct prior to that issue of having come about. Having said that, I believe that -- I have only read the case very briefly, the decision very briefly, and I haven't read the underlying briefs in support of the respective positions taken by the parties, that what is probably noteworthy is the holding, which is for the above reasons. The Chamber grants the motion in the following terms. The defendants can cross-examine a witness about pre-testimony meeting with the Prosecutor provided, and then there are the limitations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what are the limitations according to your understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: According to this is the number of preparatory meetings, the dates of meetings, and duration of meetings. The difficulty with the holding in this case, is many-folded of which I will mention but a few. First of all, it is a clear and absolute denial of the right to cross-examination under Article 21, and it directly impacts upon the accused's right to fully ventilate issues before this Chamber in its fact-finding process. Two, I believe that there is perhaps confusion on the part of the Prosecution here. And I say so for the moment both cautiously and advisedly because I haven't read the underlying briefs in support and in opposition to the motion that the -- may well be mixing up -- the Prosecution may well be mixing up or confusing the invasion into the issue of attorney work product privilege with that of what we're discussing here, which is whether or not the facts, and the facts alone, establish the potential of influence upon -- establish the potential of influence upon any particular witness. To suggest that the party inquiring into such an area must go so far as to accuse the Prosecution of misconduct misses the point. And the reason for that is very simply as follows. If, after hearing what occurred during the discussion between Mr. Nice and Mr. Sacirbey, or between the Prosecutor and any witness, as regards to the information that was discussed, the theory of the case that was being put forth, the Chamber is of the opinion that that those conversations impact upon the truth-finding process, then it's something that the Chamber can weigh in its assessment of the evidence that as being given by that particular witness. It does not have to be in any sense whatsoever misconduct. It does not have to be in any sense whatsoever done for an ill purpose. But, indeed, if the Prosecutor's manner of preparing a witness affects the structural integrity and independence of that testimony, that is something that the Chamber should take into account and should be able to take into account. Otherwise, there's virtually no reason not to have cross-examination with regard to certain issues, at all. Because have you no idea whether or not the -- the witness was influenced, at all. Or whether the witness's intent or thinking was influenced at all by virtue of the manner in which the questioning was presented. I have to tell you something, Your Honour, in all of the tapes that I have received, and in all of the verbatim, to the extent that we have received verbatim transcripts over the two cases that have I done prior to this case, I have never seen a Prosecutor engaged in a conceptual discussion with a witness about what testimony would be preferred, what testimony would be expected, what the defendant would be doing, and how best to counter such evidence. What I have seen is a Prosecutor openly and candidly asking questions about the facts of the case. Who, what, where, when, how. But not, not whatsoever, suggesting that certain areas need to be emphasised, that certain concepts need to be sought or obtained, or certain theories need to be proved. Now if that is in fact what they are doing, shame on them. If that's in fact what is going on here, shame on them. I wouldn't expect that such a thing would be going on. However, I found in the evidence what that was given to me by the Prosecution that is very clear with regard to the colloquy between Mr. Nice and Mr. Sacirbey that there was a very specific intent as regards the kinds of evidence that Mr. Nice sought that could well influence his testimony here and is something clearly that you should have available to you to consider, independent of the issue of whether or not it be deemed to be prosecutorial misconduct or not. In the state of human affairs, in the state of dialogue, in the state of conversation as between people, it is a critical component, especially when dealing with circumstantial evidence, which is one of the things you're going to be having to do, to weigh the circumstances, to make determinations about credibility, it's critical that you have an understanding of what transpired as between the parties. That's our respectful submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Two questions, or two issues. First of all, is the Chamber to make from your last rendition that you are indeed challenging the prosecutorial propriety of the Prosecutor who interviewed, Mr. Nice vis-a-vis the Milosevic case -- I beg your pardon, Mr. Sacirbey, that Prosecutor being Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I hesitate to answer the question immediately without conferring with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, when you have said shame on them, if that's what they are doing --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, absolutely. Okay. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to that issue, if that is what they are doing, indeed I am. If that's what they did, if in fact that's what they did, that they attempted to influence a witness's testimony and told a witness essentially what they required for their Prosecution -- Mr. Guy-Smith, I'm asking you whether that's what you are alleging. I'm not saying that's what they did. You have said that in your -- in the two cases that have you been involved in before questions are asked of -- in open-end form: what, where, how, when. My question is are you alleging that the discussion of concepts by Mr. Nice with Mr. Sacirbey was improper on the part of Mr. Nice to do? And if -- just yes or no, is that what are you alleging? I just want to be clear that's what you are alleging.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Since you have asked for a yes or no answer, I'm of course forced give you a yes or no answer. And my answer would be yes with an explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then the next issue that you raise in your rendition is that in terms of Article 21 of the Statute, the jurisprudence that was referred to by Madam Bolton is an absolute bar to the defence to go into that area of the testimony to test credibility. And I want to say if I -- I haven't read that decision. If I -- and I rely on counsel, what they are telling me. If what has been told so far is correct, and I have no doubt that it is, then it is not an absolute bar, because, as Madam Bolton explained, in that event, then you must make a substantiated application in your preparation to cross-examine the witness, to say, I'm going to make this application, and, therefore, I would like to go into that area. So I do not think that you you're absolutely correct when you say that it's an absolute bar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Limitations on cross-examination are always dangerous areas for the administration of justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. And in that there are limitations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There most certainly are limitations. And I would readily acknowledge that there are limitations. Having said that, limitations as they relate to issues that directly concern a fact finders assessment of the accuracy, veracity, credibility of information that they are hearing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you, Mr. Guy-Smith, because I have just indicated that you don't have an absolute bar. You have a way to deal with it. This is not a limitation at that says never, never, never. You can go around it by just following the jurisprudence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, but with regard to the jurisprudence which is -- which is one of the -- one of the reasons why I initially said that I was not familiar with those briefs that had been filed, I think it is important to note that with regard to the discussion, which is paragraph number 2 of the submissions that were made by the parties in that self-same decision, it says: "The Defence for Bizimungu recalls that during the 3rd March 2005 hearing the Prosecution objected to a question raised by the Defence for Bizimungu on the basis that the information it sought to elicit was privileged. The defence argued that there is no foundation in fact or in law that an interview between the Prosecution and the -- and a witness is confidential." We are in a distinctly factually different situation. Because in the context of our case, the information upon which I am examining was disclosed to me. Therefore, any privilege that may have existed was most assuredly waived under this particular analysis. That is a very -- it's a factually distinct situation from what we have. There, as I understand it, having briefly, very briefly read the decision, there the Prosecution said, Wait a minute, we've got a privilege here. Some format of what I would call a work-product privilege, which is an entirely different analytical discussion than a discussion where the Prosecution has given the information to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me say this. I confess to having not read this decision. The portion that was quoted certainly did not refer to privileged information. It referred to dipping into prosecutorial interviews with witnesses. And, yes, you may want to go and read the underlying motions and responses, but I guess, for purposes of jurisprudence what does guide us is the decision itself. And if the decision says you -- you may not try to find out how information was acquired by the Prosecutor from a witness, that is the jurisprudence. Whatever may have been argued. Maybe privilege was one of them, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really beg you here, I really do beg you here. I'm reading from the decision. I'm not reading what from what I call a horn-book. I'm reading from the decision itself, a horn-book, a text book of decisional law. I'm reading the decision itself. What I quoted to is from a -- [Overlapping speakers] ... so I would beg before you make a ruling here, because I think it is a point of some importance, to read the decision. So that your analysis and your ruling is predicated upon a full appreciation of what the issues were at stake there, as opposed to what I would call a cherry-picking - not on your part, but on the Prosecution's part - with regard to the holing that was made. Because the holding that was made was made in a particular factual context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... The holding, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would also -- it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I know it's time for a break. Let me just leave you with this one: That I'm not going cherry-read or cherry-pick the decision. I will look at what the decision says finally, particularly what you referred as to in it as regards its disposition. I guess this would be an appropriate time to take a break. We will come back. Hopefully we can look at the decisions during the break, and I think it is also appropriate to you dis-mute, or un-mute, or what you do?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I will request that we go back to full sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. When we come -- yeah, can we go back to full sound, so that they can hear us taking the break. Thank you very much. It seems to be time for a break. We'll take a break and come back at a quarter to 6.00, and we will rule when we come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber has had an opportunity to look at the decision, and the Chamber is in a position to give its ruling at this stage. Yes, the motions brought before the Trial Chamber III were based on privilege, to some extent. However -- and the Chamber clearly indicated that the Prosecution was out of court on privilege. However, it then said there is, however, a principle of ethnics that governs relations between interviews with -- between lawyer and a witness, and there are certain presumptions about honesty. And if we want to cross offer that border, an application should be made. That seems to me to be on all fours what we are dealing with here and not what was dealt with in that case. I would -- the Chamber would therefore rule that it does not bar the Defence from this line of questioning, provided the Defence files a motion. It doesn't have to be a motion -- yeah, Mr. Guy-Smith, I see you want to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes -- if I understand what you're your ruling is, Your Honour, is this a motion that I can make orally, or is this a motion you want in writing? How would you like me to make this motion? Because I think what I would like to do at this point in time with regard to this issue, if the Chamber wishes for me at this point in time to make such an application is, what I would like to do, is I would like to present some evidence to the Chamber and thereafter make an oral application with regard to this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As I understand the -- this decision, it calls for a substantiated application. Sorry, there's a voice that keeps coming into my ears. I don't know whether anybody hears it. Anyway, it seems that it would have to do -- [technical difficulty]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, with leave of the Chamber, what I'd like to do at this time is I would like to play a brief segment of a tape-recording that I received from the Prosecution which involves specifically a conversation between Mr. Nice and the witness. And thereafter, because I think that it will explain to the Chamber precisely what my thinking is. I don't need to have this done necessarily in front of the witness, because I don't want to influence the witness in any fashion whatsoever. But I think upon hearing the audiotape, it will be self-explanatory. This -- so the Chamber is aware, this tape -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are disconnected with New York. Did I say "with"? From.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They're still trying to reconnect. I don't know how long it would take. We will just have to wait.

utterances.text: I was just going to ask, Your Honour, are they not on mute in New York? And if so, would there be any harm in our continuing this discussion if they are muted?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: They are not on mute. We asked --

utterances.text: [Via videolink] We can hear you well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Guy-Smith, I think we're -- [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for His Honour.

utterances.text: I'm sorry, I got repeat myself. My mike was off. utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate what Your Honour has said. And let me explain to you both the dilemma and the thinking that I'm having right now. utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. We don't refuse hearing it. But it has got to be part of the application, that is for our next annex to the proper publication.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. This -- so I'm clear about what the -- I just want it make sure I'm clear about what the Chamber is going require. But you don't know whether you require that or not. If I see that to be -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fine. Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And so what I -- with that as the understanding, it seems to me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your learned friend on her feet with that as an understanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, I thought my friend had finished; he hadn't finished his thought. I do wish to have some input into this issue at some point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, we'll come back to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With that as the understanding, considering where we are, it seems to me that it would be inappropriate, based on the Court's ruling, for me to continue in this line and for me to move to some area other and then revisit this area as soon as possible, with the Chamber upon making application. The application that, at this point, I would be making, would be an ex parte application, so that the Chamber is in a position to independently view the evidence, since the application I am making is one of necessarily prosecutorial misconduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I -- obviously, the Chamber is not going to give legal advice on how to prosecute that part of the case. But, I'm just wondering why ex parte. utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand that. My legal preference would be not to have to throw down the gauntlet as far as, apparently, I do based upon the decisional law and interpretation of the Chamber, because I think there is a different basis for that. So I'm trying to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's just check again. Can you hear us down there in New York?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We can hear you, but the picture is frozen.

utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Are you happy to carry on provided can you hear us, even if we look like statues to you, or do you want to see us moving around?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm happy for you to continue. I recognise the urgency and constraints we're dealing with. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Sacirbey. Have you finished, Mr. -- yeah, you were saying something, then I said -- [Microphone not activated]

utterances.text: Excuse me -- [Microphone not activated] [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We can hear you very well, Your Honour. I'm not sure about the delay, but you sound clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith, if can you brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Surely. Understanding the situation we're in, what I am going to do at this point in time is I'm going to prepare an application. I will attach that evidence which I believe is germane to the application, and we will proceed from that point and see where it all goes. I believe that Madam Bolton has some remarks to make, but I don't know whether I need to respond to that or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, let's find out what she has got to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. In terms of the issue of it being an ex parte application, the Prosecution is opposed to that. This may be an issue where we need to confer with the person who is actually being accused of misconduct, and that individual should have a right to know what they are being accused of and an opportunity to respond. Secondly, as my friend has already indicated, I don't know what portion of which tape is he referring to, but there's clearly an issue with respect to the audibility of those tapes. So it may be that we deal with all of the cross-examination expect this area, depending on how things go. I just wanted it raise that as potential issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I -- I'm sorry, if I might respond. I think we are -- we now are really confusing the issue, and I think we are shifting what the issue is here. The issue is a really very simple issue. The issue whether or not there's prima facie evidence sufficient for the Chamber to allow me to engage in cross-examination. It has absolutely nothing to do with the person who is actually being accused of misconduct and that individual having a right or an opportunity to respond to the allegations. It seems to me one of the things is happening here, and it is unfortunate, but one of the things happening here is Ms. Bolton is concerning herself with protecting a great number of individuals who are not parties to this particular lawsuit. The fact of the matter is, either I make a prima facie showing, which is sufficient for the Chamber to allow me to engage in the examination, or I don't. And that is a factual determination which can be made on the state of the record. But I take it we're not taking a look at, at this point, the particular intent of any particular individual, which is why I said a while ago that I really was not trying to through down the gauntlet as hard as I apparently need to in order to continue this line of examination. I really -- I really find myself in an unfortunate situation because I think that the matter can be developed without having to cast aspersions or mud on anyone, but unfortunately that seems to the situation in which we are in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hear what you say. However, as I indicated earlier, as soon as you mentioned ex parte, I expressed my doubts. I do not think this is a matter to be dealt with ex parte. Irrespective of whether or not the Prosecution would consult with Mr. Nice, I think they still have a right to respond to -- to your motion, and you to reply. utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. With all of the rulings and guidance of the Chamber, I will proceed with my examination in an area that is slightly different from that which I have been in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Guy-Smith. You can still hear us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You may proceed, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to move now to a slightly -- a different issue, as I think you understand we need to do at this time. And I'm going to start with an understanding with you, if I could, of when you became the ambassador to the United Nations for Bosnia-Herzegovina. As I understand what you've told us, prior to the time that Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised in the United Nations by resolution, you had been working with the government. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the date that Bosnia-Herzegovina became part of -- I'm sorry, was recognised, I believe you told us, was the 22nd of May. True?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we should be specific here. 1992.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, before Bosnia-Herzegovina became recognised as an independent state by the United Nations, there was some concern as to whether or not you were going to be tied up in terms of being recognised; correct? Do you follow what I'm --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. In that regard, you learned before the time of the passing of the resolution that there was a plan afoot to keep Bosnia-Herzegovina from being recognised in the United Nations; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a plan afoot to delay recognition potentially beyond that of Slovenia and Croatia. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Correct. And that is -- excuse me. And that is information that you obtained, I believe, from the representative of Turkey?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is one of the sources. It's actually not the representative of Turkey but a Turkish national who was a representative of the organisation of the Islamic conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, the Turkish national who was a representative of the organisation of the Islamic conference, that particular individual, do you by any chance, as we sit here -- or as you sit here, and I stand, have his name in mind?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It is right on the tip of my tongue. But you'll excuse me, if it just doesn't come to me right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's fine. And above and beyond or that, or in addition to that particular gentleman being involved in this particular concern, if I'm not mistaken, there was also the former ambassador of Saudi Arabia, who was involved in the concern of the delay of the independence of resolution being passed; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the individual you are referring to was the president of the General Assembly who happened to be also the former ambassador of Saudi Arabia, and also the representative of Austria was another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to this particular issue, and that is the issue of whether or not the resolution would be delayed for technical reasons, you were made a commitment, and I believe both you and Dr. Silajdzic were made a commitment, that the other two countries would not be admitted into the General Assembly until Bosnia was also admitted; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would prefer to define it as a package, that Bosnia, Croatia, and Slovenia would be admitted at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me refer you to page 35 of the transcript with regard to the meeting that you had with Mr. Nice. And I'm referring you to page -- to lines 20 through -- through 27 where you say, according to the transcript that was provided to us by the Prosecutor: "He made a commitment to Dr. Silajdzic and myself that the other two countries would not be admitted. He would not allow those of the General Assembly until Bosnia was also admitted."

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think -- I think, Mr. Guy-Smith, I said I preferred to define it as.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I understand that you say you would prefer to define it is as, and apparently it has not come up on the screen, and I do -- that's -- what's the number? That's, once again, 1D03-1325 at page 35 of 62. And there we go, yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it front of me, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. That's what you told -- that's what you told Mr. Nice at the time; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, when that occurred, was that something that occurred in a public session, with other participants of the United Nations? Is that something that occurred in private session? Was a hallway conversation? How did this come about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When what occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When what occurred?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROHAN
utterances.text: When the commitment was made by the gentleman that he would not allow the other two countries to become -- to be recognised as being independent in front of the General Assembly unless Bosnia was also included. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You said had you a meeting, I think?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, we had meetings with several ambassadors along the same point, as I mentioned Austria, several others, United States. We definitely did receive a commitment from the president of the General Assembly, who, as I pointed out, was a former ambassador of Saudi Arabia to the United Nations. And this was one of those private meetings, or one might say, official but private meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to this official but private meeting, as you have characterized it, I take it that you were present, Dr. Silajdzic was present, as well as the president of the General Assembly, with regard to that particular meeting. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now with regard to that particular meeting, did you have occasion to make any notes of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have, Mr. Guy-Smith, but usually if I would have kept notes, there would have been maybe to the effect of two, three, five, sentences at most.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to -- with regard to that, and this will become a, so you know, continuing question, do you have any -- as you sit here today, do you have any of the notes that you may have taken or that did you take throughout that period of time today?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not believe that I do. Unless they happen to be casually inserted so some other document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you also mentioned that you had a meeting with, I believe, the representative of Austria; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And who would that have been?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the ambassador's name escapes me. But we actually, even at that time, made use of the premises of the mission of Austria in order to be able to address various bureaucratic issues, i.e., providing papers, drafting documents, whatever may have been necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, and you also mentioned that you had, I take it, a similar conversation with regard to this particular resolution not being passed unless all three countries were involved in it with the representative of the United States of America?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had several meetings with not necessarily the ambassador but with Jr. representatives. I personally remember meetings involving everything from the representative of Japan to other representatives on the Security Council primarily. I would be a little bit hard-pressed to remember all of the ambassadors that we met with or that I may have met with by myself. The you are urgency of Bosnia's admission to the United Nations, though, was a primary topic at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And as I understand the situation at that time, there were efforts being made by the then Secretary-General, Boutros Boutros-Ghali, from keeping Bosnia from being recognised at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a characterization that I'm not prepared to acknowledge. I believe there were efforts that we suspected were given some information, but I think that would be probably an unfair conclusion on my part. I don't have absolute first-hand knowledge, although I do have some information.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with regard to that, if we once again have the same document up on the screen and the same page.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm referring you to line -- referring you to line 29, you told Mr. Nice, did you not, that, and I quote the language here: "The last effort to stop Bosnia from being admitted was that the Secretary-General Boutros-Ghali - so I've had indiscernible conversations since then about a lot of these events ..." I take it what you referred to then was what you've just alluded to now with regard to the United Nations Secretary-General being involved in at least delaying the process of Bosnia-Herzegovina being recognised by the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I'm referring there that obviously there were conversations that I've had since then which pointed as the Secretary-General being one of the potential stumbling-blocks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So I understand this, because I had a distinctly different impression of how the United Nations worked a couple of weeks ago when we were talking, and perhaps you can be of some assistance here. From what I understand, you had a minimum of three separate meetings with representatives from member states concerning, and I use the word advisedly, but concerning a deal to be made in order for your -- constituency to be recognised by the United Nations. This wasn't something that happened in public, was it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, perhaps I can clarify by exactly relating to you the events of that moment, which was that Bosnia and Herzegovina had forwarded an application to the Secretary-General's office, as it is bound to, for admission to the United Nations. Upon receiving the call from the gentleman that I referred to, the representative of the OIC, I was told that in fact there might be some problems with our application. I immediately took it upon myself to try to locate the status of our application within the Secretary-General's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could I stop you there for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: When refer here to Secretary-General Boutros-Ghali, I'm referring to his office --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could I stop you there for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: And to be very blunt --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could I stop there for a moment, sir. Could I stop you there for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... please --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Because I would really like to understand your answer here.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You said, Upon receiving the call from the gentleman that I referred to, the representative of the OIC, I was told in fact there might be some problems with our application. Now was the gentleman who you talked to from the OIC, is he part of some kind of vetting committee that makes a determination whether or not your application is in order for purposes of it becoming a resolution?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just recall the gentleman's name. It's Enjin Ansaj [phoen]. And, no, I don't believe so, and I, frankly, had never met the gentleman before until I received the call. He just made the point that there seemed to have been some problem with our application. And to use a term that we use here often in America, something was not kosher.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, and when something was not kosher, I take it that what you're saying is that there was some belief, and I'm asking you the question now, when something is not kosher in a political sense, there is usually some kind of conspiracy afoot with regard to what is going on. Is that what you're referring to? There was some -- some conspiracy or some decision made by other member states in terms of denying Bosnia-Herzegovina the ability to be recognised by the General Assembly of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any conspiracy. I'm aware of the fact that when I contacted the Secretary General's office, I was told that in fact our application was in office A, then office B, ultimately turned out that it was misplaced. And actually we, at that moment, made a new application and presented it to the Secretary General on a moment's notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why that problem developed, I have been told several stories. Which of those stories is absolutely accurate, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Can you help us at all with the fact that you were receiving information from an individual who you had never met before, who was the representative of the organisation of the Islamic council with regard to this particular issue? Do you have any information about how that occurred --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If in fact -- well, actually I do remember that at that time, the call had came through the mission of Austria, because that's where, in fact, we had been meeting, and somehow he tracked us down. You'll recall, of course, this was the time before cell phones or at least some sort of mass use of cell phones.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to this -- this particular issue, it sounds like there -- and I'm asking you once again, and you're certainly in a better position than I am to -- to explain this. It sounds like there was some argument that was going on between a number of parties with regard to this particular matter, which is the resolution being passed. Can you help out at all in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Absolutely, Mr. Guy-Smith. I think we're talking, though, about two separate issues that may have been related. And certainly when I'm -- when I'm looking upon these issues, one is that, clearly, there was a discussion as to whether or not Bosnia and Herzegovina should be admitted at the same time as Croatia and Slovenia. On the other hand there seemed to have been at least some sort of, one would say, bureaucratic screw-up where an application dually made, in fact, could not at first be located. And then only subsequent to our extensive searches was it located, and we were told, Well, there might be some problem with the fact that it was faxed from Sarajevo rather than delivered -- hand-delivered or provided by mail. We took very quick action to provide a new application immediately signed by Dr. Silajdzic who was empowered to do that on behalf of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, to what extent these issues are linked, certainly did raise some concerns, if you would, even suspicions. Was there a conspiracy? I'm not certainly not prepared to go to that length at all. And finally the issue was resolved. So I'm happy to say that subsequent information that I received did indicate that maybe something was not kosher. Did I ever get to the bottom of it? Not really. Did I feel it was a relevant item to raise in my interview with the Prosecution? Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you for that -- I thank you for that answer. With regard to what happened before this -- this particular incident, I understand that you had a meeting with Mr. Vance concerning the issue of the referendum. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. That occurred actually several months -- yes, I do. Several months earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to the issue of the referendum, as I'm sure you are aware, the question of the referendum dealt with the specific issue of who was going to vote for what particular state; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm trying to make it as general as I can for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's -- let's assume it was the about the future status of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. In that regard, when you met with Mr. Vance --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, you know the screen here is gone blank, but I can hear you just fine, so I'm happy to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. If you're happy to continue, so am I. If you're not, then I'll deal with that too. But since you said you are, that's fine. Now, in your discussion with Mr. Vance, there was no question as to whether or not the referendum itself was proper; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And so as you've characterized it before, before you met with Mr. Vance, the issue of the propriety of the referendum was already a fate accompli; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When referring to Mr. Vance, for purposes of record, since we have both been discussing this gentleman's name, who are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about a gentleman that has passed away, a very distinguished US diplomat named Cyrus Vance, and he was at that acting in a capacity as a Special Representative for the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And at that point in time when was acting in the special capacity, he, that is, Mr. Vance had made a determination that he felt this was an appropriate way to go, and by that I mean the referendum was an appropriate way to proceed forward; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the meeting that I attended, and this was in February of 1992, that I believe is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now with regard to that meeting that you had with him, the issue of a potential boycott came up. And if I'm not mistaken, it did not cause Mr. Vance any concerns with regard to potentially delaying or not going ahead with the election; correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not sure to what extent this witness can comment on what concerns -- what the mental state was of Cyrus Vance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, I would be more than happy to rephrase the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could please have the same document again at page 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I'm referring to you line 14 in which you said to Mr. Nice, and I quote: "The emphasis of course was to try to get all the Bosnians to vote, but when the issue of potential sort of boycott came about, and it did not in any way cause Mr. Vance to say, We should delay or not go ahead with the elections." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that statement -- yes, that statement is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And then you went on to tell Mr. Nice, with regard to this particular meeting: "That the meeting with the Secretary General was more perfunctory, but in both instances, it was clear that a referendum for independence was almost a foregone conclusion. And what was really needed to be done was chart the course of how we get from the referendum to the actual form of independence." Right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So with regard to this meeting that you had with Mr. Vance, do you know who else was privy to the determination that had been made concerning that there would be a referendum for independence?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I'm -- the reason I'm asking you the question --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean from --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking the question is, with regard to the matter we were referring to beforehand, it seemed that there were - shall we put it this way - a lot of ears to the ground who had information concerning with a was going on, and by that I'm referring to the delay of the resolution for your independence. By you, I'm talking obviously about Bosnia-Herzegovina. So I'm wondering if you know whether or not the same kind of information was available to other nation states or members of the United Nations, with regard to the fact that it had been decided that there would be a referendum for independence, irrespective of a boycott?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Guy-Smith, we're talking about the referendum taking place at the very end of February. And when we're talking about Bosnia's admission to the United Nations, these critical moments discussed beforehand was really in mid-May.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Yes, absolutely, but what I'm referring to is the nature of the kind of conversation, not the time of the conversation, but the fact that there seems to be a number of private conversations between member states to which the General Assembly or the Security Council is not necessarily privy to in which major international decisions are being made.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're talking about the continuing negotiations that were held in various parts mostly of Europe regarding the status of Bosnia and Herzegovina during this period of time, I'm well aware of those occurring. However, I did not attend, nor did I receive any sort of briefing at that time. I was not a Bosnian official. Frankly, I didn't even think that I would be. I thought I was helping rather than taking on a responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I am here. I was reading your answer. There was a word that I didn't pick up, but I'm fine now. Thank you. Ultimately, the resolution passed, and Bosnia became a member state; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. We were actually sponsored by Finland.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when it became a member state, it was, of course, subject to all of the rules and regulations of the United Nations. True?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to resolutions that had been passed beforehand, before it became a member state, there was a particular resolution that caused, shall we say, not only discussion, but also great concern, as far as you were -- as far as you were concerned, with regard to an embargo. True?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I am referring to Resolution 713, which is Exhibit P2431. Now, with regard to Resolution 71 --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the Resolution 713 --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't know about anyone else, but I just have Mr. Guy-Smith on my screen and not New York. Is it just me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Welcome to the club. And I thought I heard Mr. Sacirbey start a sentence and getting cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I seem to be -- well, I was frozen in time, and then I'm not, and then I am.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If -- we could still hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirbey, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Wonderful. We were discussing 713. And as I understand Resolution 713, it was a total embargo in the area including Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The language was on Yugoslavia which was subsequently deemed to be the territory of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to -- with regard to Resolution 713, can you tell us, is it your understanding that 713 was a resolution passed under chapter 7?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, and as I understand your position and your understanding of chapter 7, chapter 7 made the resolution mandatory for member states; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And certainly by the 22nd of May, Bosnia-Herzegovina was a member state; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And as a matter of fact, and we will be discussing this more fully as -- as time goes on in our conversation, this was a matter that you constantly and repeatedly raised with the various members of the General Assembly and the Security Council, which was the lifting of the provisions of 713 as against Bosnia-Herzegovina with no success; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I would agree with just that last part of the statement, with no success, but certainly that was the focus of one of our diplomatic efforts, certainly a high priority.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But with regard to the issue of no success, it's certainly something that was not available to you in the calendar years of 1992, 1993, 1994 and a considerable part of 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But diplomatic initiatives sometimes have results that are not necessarily direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, when you say -- when you say that diplomatic initiatives sometimes have results that are not necessarily direct, could you please explain what you mean by that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were states that ultimately took the view that Resolution 713 was not binding upon Bosnia-Herzegovina because it had been adopted before Bosnia and Herzegovina was a member state, and because Bosnia and Herzegovina was faced with a direct assault upon its sovereignty and territorial integrity and, in fact, its primary right to defend itself was the one that legally dominated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And is that -- the matter that you just -- you've just raised is, that a matter that was accepted by the Security Council with regard to the mandatory provisions under chapter 7 or is what you're --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- or is what you're telling us now that various states interpreted the law as they chose to and acted accordingly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I think the last statement that you made is largely correct. Second of all, again I emphasise the resolution never defined Bosnia and Herzegovina as someone that was subject directly to the arms embargo, and certainly not under the conditions of being under direct assault and genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, now the last --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just understanding something here. Mr. Sacirbey, a little earlier you said the resolution applied to - its mentioned Yugoslavia, thereby referring to the former Yugoslavia. Did it exclude Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not explicitly, Your Honour. When the resolution was adopted, there was never a view that Yugoslavia would become several different countries, at least the way I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So how do you then say Bosnia and Herzegovina was excluded from this resolution? I don't understand what you mean if --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour -- Your Honour, I don't believe I've ever said in my testimony that Bosnia-Herzegovina was excluded. I'm saying, in fact, was Bosnia and Herzegovina included? And my view is that Bosnia and Herzegovina, because it had not been a member state at the time that the resolution was adopted, and because, also, at that time it had been under direct assault and its population was threatened by genocide, in fact, was not covered by that resolution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I used the word "excluded," I mean that [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- not covered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My apologies if I mischaracterized your answer, but that very point you are making, the argument you are making that Bosnia and Herzegovina was not a member state, certainly, that doesn't exclude it and in any case if the former Yugoslavia as a whole country is affected by the resolution. So whether or not Bosnia is a member state becomes irrelevant, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not necessarily Your Honour because part of Bosnia's obligation, as well as right, once it is a member state, a sovereign state, is that to defend its territorial integrity and sovereignty, and now it has a distinct obligation to defend its population. When it was a part of the former Yugoslavia as a whole, that distinct obligation did not exist in terms of the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So we were faced with what amounted to an inept challenge to our territory -- an inept, I should say, effort to defend our population as well as our sovereignty and territorial integrity from the international community and, at the same time, we had an obligation, as a state, to defend that sovereignty and territorial integrity, and particularly defend the population therein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So clearly there were some contradictions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. So my -- am I understanding correctly, the interpretation of the resolution then was: This resolution was passed with respect to the former Yugoslavia, at the time Bosnia-Herzegovina was not an independent state. Now that Bosnia-Herzegovina is an independent state it acquires rights and obligations, amongst them the right to defend itself; therefore, it gets extricated from the obligations of former Yugoslavia. It assumes its own obligations as an independent state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour, and especially in view of the reality it continued from May 22nd to the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just wanted to understand how your thinking goes on this line. Thank you so much. I'm sorry, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Not a problem, at all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I take it since you've taken that position with regard to Bosnia-Herzegovina, the same would be true for the other former parts of Yugoslavia that became independent states. They, too would --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be for those states --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: They, too would -- had --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be for those states to assert and, of course, for what purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, if you can repeat that answer again. We didn't hear you, "... that would be for those states ..."?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I -- it would be -- that right and obligation, of course, would be for those states to assert and, of course, the purpose of that. I am explicitly tying Bosnia's view on this to the defence against an actual war and what we saw as a genocide going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And so -- so we're clear, the view that you have expressed here, if I understand your testimony correctly, is a view that if they chose to, would have similarly been expressed by Slovenia, Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could have been, yes. Could have been, yes. I would prefer not to speak on their behalf although I think they were at least [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, what I'm getting at is a general proposition.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... adopting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What I'm getting at is a general proposition that you're suggesting was available for analysis which is that although the provision under chapter 7 was mandatory with regard to the former Yugoslavia, there were exceptions to the mandatory provisions of this resolution by virtue of the analysis that you've just engaged in?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I they think we can safely say that Slovenia was completely free of conflict at that time and Croatia was largely at least -- yes, but I think that would be probably a pretty accurate state.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to what we're referring to the here, we're referring to the issue of member states because chapter 7 specifically applies to member states; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you were -- oh, my goodness. You were not trained -- the oh my goodness was looking at the time, my friend. You were not trained as a diplomat; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And were you ever made aware of the statement that was made by -- I believe it was Mr. Owen in a book that he wrote, and if I could, I'm going to pull it up for you so I could get it properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that's going to be 1D00-1843, which is going to be...

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Tab?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I'm referring to Lord David Owen, a gentleman whom I believe you knew; correct? And I'm referring to page --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, I have something that looks like it's written by Marjan Malesic at that tab.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct. And go to page --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] That's what we have as well, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Go to page 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Page 25, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Which going to be 26 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Nothing --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm quite confused. I thought we were talking about something that Lord Owen had written.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. Bear with me and all will come out in the wash.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In the very first paragraph of his book --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Go down, scroll down, please. Further, further, further. Beautiful.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Balkan Odyssey, Owen emphasised that: "Nothing is simple in the Balkans. History pervades everything and complexities confound even the most careful study. Never before in over 30 years of public life have I had to operate in such a climate of dishonour, propaganda, and dissembling. Many of the people with whom I've had to deal with in the former Yugoslavia were literally strangers to the truth." Are you familiar with that particular statement of Lord Owen?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we actually even talked about it once or twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would this be an appropriate time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It would be a perfect time. We stand adjourned to tomorrow, the 30th of June at 2.00 -- quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon. Court adjourned.
